problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict:** I have found a complete solution.  
The minimum number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Notation:** Let the uncovered squares be \((i,\sigma(i))\) for a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(n=2025\).  
   The cells left of each uncovered square form the set  

   \[
   L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;1\le j<\sigma(i)\},
   \]

   and the cells right of each uncovered square form  

   \[
   R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;\sigma(i)<j\le n\}.
   \]

2. **Upper bound (construction):**  
   For every row \(i\) place a rectangle covering columns \(1,\dots ,\sigma(i)-1\) (if \(\sigma(i)>1\)) and a rectangle covering columns \(\sigma(i)+1,\dots ,n\) (if \(\sigma(i)<n\)).  
   These are disjoint \(1\times(\sigma(i)-1)\) and \(1\times(n-\sigma(i))\) tiles.  
   Exactly one row has \(\sigma(i)=1\) and one row has \(\sigma(i)=n\); all other rows receive two tiles.  
   Hence the construction uses  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2=4048
   \]

   tiles and satisfies the “one uncovered square per row and column’’ condition.

3. **Lower bound (optimality):**  
   *Lemma 1.* The left region \(L\) cannot be tiled with fewer than \(n-1\) rectangles.  
   *Proof by induction on \(n\):*  
   – Base \(n=1\): \(L\) is empty, requiring \(0=n-1\) tiles.  
   – Inductive step: let \(r\) be the unique row with \(\sigma(r)=n\).  
     The cell \((r,n-1)\in L\) must belong to a tile \(T\).  
     Because any other row \(i\neq r\) has \(\sigma(i)\le n-1\), its left interval ends at column \(\le n-2\); thus column \(n-1\) is not present in that row.  
     Consequently \(T\) cannot contain any row other than \(r\); it is the \(1\times(n-1)\) rectangle covering the whole left interval of row \(r\).  
     Removing row \(r\) and column \(n\) leaves an \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) instance with permutation \(\sigma'\) on the remaining rows and columns.  
     By the induction hypothesis the reduced left region needs at least \((n-2)\) rectangles; together with \(T\) we need at least \((n-1)\) rectangles for \(L\). ∎  

   *Lemma 2.* By horizontal symmetry the right region \(R\) also needs at least \(n-1\) rectangles.  

   Since a tile cannot intersect both \(L\) and \(R\) (it would have to cover the uncovered square \((i,\sigma(i))\)), the total number of tiles required to cover the whole grid is at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2.
   \]

4. **Conclusion:** The construction uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles, and the lower‑bound lemmas show that no tiling can use fewer. Therefore the minimum number of tiles is \(\boxed{4048}\).

---

**### Detailed Solution ###  

Let  

\[
n=2025,\qquad 
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid 1\le i\le n\}
\]

be the set of uncovered unit squares, where \(\sigma\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).  
Every row \(i\) contains exactly the uncovered square \((i,\sigma(i))\); every column \(j\) contains exactly the uncovered square \((\sigma^{-1}(j),j)\).

Define the two disjoint regions

\[
L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;1\le j<\sigma(i)\},
\qquad
R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i\le n,\;\sigma(i)<j\le n\}.
\]

All unit squares that must be covered are precisely \(L\cup R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  An explicit tiling with \(2n-2\) tiles  

For each row \(i\) do the following.

* If \(\sigma(i)>1\) place the rectangle  

  \[
  T_i^{\text{left}}=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j\le \sigma(i)-1\},
  \]

  a \(1\times(\sigma(i)-1)\) tile covering the whole left interval of the row.

* If \(\sigma(i)<n\) place the rectangle  

  \[
  T_i^{\text{right}}=\{(i,j)\mid \sigma(i)+1\le j\le n\},
  \]

  a \(1\times(n-\sigma(i))\) tile covering the whole right interval of the row.

The two tiles in a given row lie on opposite sides of the uncovered square \((i,\sigma(i))\); therefore they are disjoint.  Tiles belonging to different rows occupy distinct rows, so no two tiles overlap.  Consequently the collection  

\[
\mathcal T=\{T_i^{\text{left}}\mid \sigma(i)>1\}\cup\{T_i^{\text{right}}\mid \sigma(i)<n\}
\]

covers exactly \(L\cup R\).

Exactly one row satisfies \(\sigma(i)=1\) (the row whose uncovered square lies in column 1) and exactly one row satisfies \(\sigma(i)=n\) (the row whose uncovered square lies in column \(n\)).  Hence

\[
|\mathcal T|=\bigl|\{i\mid\sigma(i)>1\}\bigr|
                +\bigl|\{i\mid\sigma(i)<n\}\bigr|
           =(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2.
\]

For \(n=2025\) this yields a tiling with \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\) tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  A lower bound of \(2n-2\) tiles  

We prove that any tiling of \(L\cup R\) satisfying the problem’s conditions uses at least \(2n-2\) tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### Lemma 1 (left side)

*Claim.*  The region \(L\) cannot be tiled with fewer than \(n-1\) axis‑aligned rectangles.

*Proof.*  Induction on \(n\).

*Base \(n=1\).*  Then \(L=\varnothing\); the claim holds because \(0=n-1\).

*Inductive step.*  Assume the statement true for all sizes smaller than \(n\) (\(n\ge2\)).  
Let \(r\) be the unique row with \(\sigma(r)=n\).  In row \(r\) the left interval consists of the cells \((r,1),\dots,(r,n-1)\); in particular \((r,n-1)\in L\).

Let \(T\) be the tile covering \((r,n-1)\).  Because \(T\) is a rectangle, its column interval contains column \(n-1\).  For any other row \(i\neq r\) we have \(\sigma(i)\le n-1\); consequently its left interval ends at column \(\sigma(i)-1\le n-2\) and does **not** contain column \(n-1\).  Hence \(T\) cannot contain any row other than \(r\); otherwise it would also contain a cell \((i,n-1)\notin L\).  Therefore  

\[
T=\{(r,j)\mid 1\le j\le n-1\},
\]

the \(1\times(n-1)\) rectangle covering the entire left interval of row \(r\).

Delete row \(r\) and column \(n\) from the board, and delete the tile \(T\).  The remaining uncovered squares form a permutation \(\sigma'\) of the set \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{r\}\) on the \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) board, and the remaining part of \(L\) is exactly the left region associated with \(\sigma'\).  By the induction hypothesis this reduced left region needs at least \((n-2)\) rectangles.  Adding the rectangle \(T\) gives a total of at least  

\[
1+(n-2)=n-1
\]

rectangles for the original region \(L\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### Lemma 2 (right side)

*Claim.*  The region \(R\) also requires at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

*Proof.*  Apply Lemma 1 to the horizontally reflected board, i.e. replace each column index \(j\) by \(n+1-j\).  This swaps left and right sides while preserving all combinatorial properties.  The reflected permutation is again a permutation, so Lemma 1 yields the required bound for \(R\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
##### Completion of the lower bound

A tile cannot intersect both \(L\) and \(R\); otherwise it would contain the uncovered square \((i,\sigma(i))\) that separates the two regions, contradicting the rule that uncovered squares are not covered.  Hence the set of tiles used to cover the whole board is the disjoint union of a family covering \(L\) and a family covering \(R\).  By Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 each family contains at least \(n-1\) rectangles.  Consequently any admissible tiling uses at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Determination of the minimum

The construction of Section 1 uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles, and the lower‑bound argument of Section 2 shows that no tiling can use fewer.  Therefore the minimum possible number of tiles is

\[
\boxed{2n-2}=\boxed{4048}.
\]

For the original \(2025\times2025\) grid the answer is \(\boxed{4048}\).
